name: Alberti (proper)
description: low-high-mid-high, the bass note RE-ARTICULATED, not a held drone: `A2e E3e C3e E3e A2e E3e C3e E3e`. Light, transparent. Best for lyrical themes. Don't run it for more than ~4 bars unbroken.

name: Oom-pah (the Classical default, lighter than Alberti)
description: bass on beats 1 & 3, chord on 2 & 4: `D2q [D3,F3,A3]q A2q [D3,F3,A3]q`. The single most idiomatic Classical accompaniment. Bass LEAPS between root and fifth; the off-beat chord is mid-register.

name: Oom-pah-pah / waltz-feel in 4
description: bass then two chords: `D2e [F3,A3]e [F3,A3]e ...`

name: Broken / murky octaves (Sturm und Drang motor)
description: the D-minor storm engine, alternating octave tremolo: `D2s D3s D2s D3s ...` or `D2e D3e D2e D3e D2e D3e D2e D3e`. Use for dramatic, driving passages — this is what K.466 uses, NOT static-pedal Alberti.

name: Repeated chords (pulsing)
description: `[D3,F3,A3]e` ×8, or quarter pulses. Gives weight without melodic figuration. Good under a busy RH.

name: Walking / scalar bass
description: quarter or eighth notes stepping through the harmony: `D2q E2q F2q G2q` — drives transitions and sequences.

name: Sustained / held
description: LH holds a chord or octave for the whole bar while the RH carries everything: `[D2,D3]w` or `[D3,A3,D4]w`. ESSENTIAL for breathing — use it where the RH is active or at a phrase peak.

name: Unison / octave doubling with RH
description: both hands strike the same line for a bare, dramatic tutti stroke (theme statements, climaxes): LH mirrors the RH an octave or two below.

name: LH rest / drop-out
description: the LH is SILENT for a beat or a bar (rest), letting the RH ring or breathe. Mozart uses silence constantly. A `rest` in the LH is not a bug.

name: Two-voice / contrapuntal bass
description: a real melodic line in the LH answering the RH (varied recaps, developments).

name: Alberti bass
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Murky bass (octave alternation)
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Waltz bass (3/4, L:1/8)
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Parallel thirds & sixths
description: the signature Mozart sweetness for lyrical themes. Double the melody a 3rd or 6th below in the same rhythm: `[F5,A5]q [E5,G5]e [D5,F5]e ...`. Use across lyrical second themes and consoling passages. Don't overuse in stormy material.

name: Appoggiatura "sigh"
description: a dissonance ON the strong beat resolving DOWN by step on the weak beat, slurred two-note: `(G5q F5q)` over an F chord (the G leans, the F resolves). The emotional core of Mozart's minor-key writing. Place at phrase peaks and cadential approaches.

name: Cadential trill
description: a trill on scale-degree 2 (or the dominant note) approaching a PAC, ideally with a turned suffix: `A5h:tr` then resolve to the tonic. Reserve for real cadences (PAC, important HC), not every bar.

name: Turns & mordents
description: a gruppetto (turn) wrapping a sustained melody note `:turn`, a mordent `:mord` on an accented note. Ornament arrivals and long notes, not running passages.

name: Grace-note appoggiatura
description: a short `:grace` note leaning into a strong beat from a step above. Adds vocal inflection at phrase starts/peaks.

name: Echo dynamics (terraced repetition)
description: state a 1-2 bar idea `f`, then immediately repeat it (often an octave up or same register) `p`. A quintessential Mozart/Classical gesture. Great for presentation phrases and codettas. Mark the dynamics explicitly.

name: Triplet contrast
description: break prevailing duple (eighths/sixteenths) with a bar or two of triplet figuration for rhythmic variety and forward lilt.

name: Scale flourish as punctuation
description: a fast run is connective/cadential tissue, used ONCE to drive into an arrival — not the default surface. If a phrase is >55% stepwise, replace some runs with arpeggios/leaps.

name: Leap-to-peak then step-down
description: approach a registral apex by leap (6th, octave, arpeggio), then release it by step. Gives the line a profile and a clear high point.

name: Periodic structure
description: antecedent (4 bars, ends on a HC, "question") + consequent (4 bars, begins like the antecedent, ends PAC, "answer"). Make the consequent's opening RECOGNIZABLY echo the antecedent.

name: Sentence structure
description: presentation (a 2-bar basic idea + its repetition, often sequenced up a step or varied) → continuation (fragment the idea, accelerate harmonic rhythm) → cadence. Mozart's primary themes are often sentences.

name: Deceptive feint
description: approach the cadence, then resolve V→vi instead of V→I once, before finally landing the real PAC. Adds a moment of surprise.

name: Cadential 6/4
description: at important cadences: I6/4 → V(7) → I. Lean the 6/4 on a strong beat (it's a dominant-function suspension).

name: Feminine cadence
description: resolve the final tonic on a WEAK beat (e.g. beat 2), often after an appoggiatura. Gentler than a downbeat slam; very Mozart for lyrical endings.

name: Neapolitan (bII6)
description: in minor, a flat-supertonic-sixth chord for a dark expressive stab before the dominant. Let it land (fp, slight hold).

name: Two-part texture, bass as a real line
description: often just a single melodic line under the melody, no chords at all: `C3q D3q E3q F3q`. Haydn writes far more two-voice keyboard texture than Mozart, and it is the most under-used idiom in generated Classical writing.

name: Oom-pah, dry
description: `C2q [E3,G3]q C2q [E3,G3]q`. Present, but lighter and more often staccato than in Mozart. The dots matter: without them it is heavy.

name: Alberti
description: used, but Haydn tires of it faster. Two to four bars, then something else.

name: The sudden rest
description: `rest_h [G2,B2,D3]h`, or a whole bar of silence in the middle of a phrase. Haydn's signature. A joke needs a beat of nothing before the punchline.

name: Repeated notes as a drone
description: the same bass note pulsing under changing harmony above: `G2e ×8`. The rustic, folk-derived sound of the finales; suggests a drone instrument.

name: Bare octaves for emphasis
description: `[C2,C3]h` at the start of a phrase or a development, with nothing in between. Stark and attention-getting.

name: Off-beat entries
description: the accompaniment begins on beat 2 rather than beat 1: `rest_q [C3,E3,G3]q [C3,E3,G3]q [C3,E3,G3]q`. Displaces the whole bar's feeling without changing a note of the melody.

name: Walking bass into a cadence
description: quarters stepping down to the dominant over two bars. Straightforward, and it is what makes his cadences sound inevitable.

name: Hand crossing / bass above the melody
description: occasionally the left hand plays *above* the right for a bar or two. A colour effect, and unmistakably his.

name: Unison passages
description: both hands on the same line, often at the start of a development or after a fermata. Bare and dramatic in a way the galant style otherwise avoids.

name: Held chord under a running right hand
description: `[C3,E3,G3]w`. Simple, and it gives the right hand room to be virtuosic.

name: The general pause
description: everything stops mid-phrase, for a beat or a whole bar, then the music resumes. His signature, and it appears in most fast movements.

name: The false recapitulation
description: the theme returns in the wrong key, is allowed to continue for a few bars, and is then corrected. The listener is caught out twice: once by the early return and once by its being wrong.

name: The extra bar
description: a four-bar phrase becomes five because one bar is repeated, or seven because the cadence is delayed. Hyper-regular phrase rhythm is not his; irregularity is.

name: The repeated cadence
description: a phrase cadences, then cadences again, then a third time, each slightly different. Comic when fast, emphatic when slow.

name: The sudden dynamic
description: one bar of `pp` in the middle of a forte passage, or a `ff` chord after a long quiet stretch (the "Surprise" gesture, and it works because everything before it is regular).

name: Ending on the wrong thing
description: a movement that stops on a dominant, or on a fragment, or simply trails off. He does not always close firmly.

name: The wrong-key opening
description: beginning somewhere other than the tonic and arriving at it a few bars in.

name: Monothematicism
description: the second subject is the first subject in the dominant. Write one good theme and re-use it rather than inventing a second.

name: Motivic development from a tiny cell
description: like Beethoven, but wittier: the fragment is turned over, inverted, and handed between the hands.

name: Two-part texture
description: melody and a single bass line, no chords at all, for whole phrases. Far more common in Haydn than in Mozart and one of the cheapest ways to make a texture change.

name: Folk-derived material
description: drone fifths, modal inflections, and dance rhythms, especially in finales. The rustic register is deliberate.

name: Hand crossing
description: the left hand plays above the right for a bar or two. A colour effect and unmistakably his.

name: Unison passages
description: both hands on the same line for a bare, attention-getting statement, usually at a development's opening.

name: Ornament as punctuation
description: a turn or a trill placed at the *end* of a gesture rather than on a long note, closing it off like a spoken inflection.

name: The rhetorical question
description: a phrase that ends on a rising interval, on the dominant, unanswered, followed by a pause.

name: Remote modulation by common tone
description: one note is held while the harmony around it changes into an unexpected key.

name: Deceptive cadence used comically
description: the resolution avoided and then immediately made fun of by repetition.

name: Long dominant preparation, then the theme arrives early
description: the setup and the payoff deliberately mismatched.

name: Minore variation
description: in a variation set, one variation in the parallel minor, usually more chromatic and more serious than its neighbours.

name: Sudden chromatic side-step
description: in an otherwise diatonic passage, held for one bar, then corrected.

name: Repeated-chord motor
description: the engine of the driving movements. Straight eighths or sixteenths on one chord: `[C3,Eb3,G3]e ×8`. Relentless, and it *accumulates*: what makes it Beethoven rather than Alberti is that it does not decorate, it insists. Use under a melody that is itself agitated.

name: Broken octaves / murky bass
description: `C2s C3s C2s C3s …`. The storm engine (Op.13 first movement, Op.31/2). Wider and heavier than a tremolo; the two notes are an octave apart and the effect is a low growl, not a shimmer.

name: Rising bass line against a static melody
description: quarters or half notes climbing chromatically or by step while the right hand holds: `C2h C#2h`, `D2h Eb2h`. This is how Beethoven builds tension without getting louder, and it is almost absent from generated writing.

name: The LH takes the theme
description: the motif moves to the bass while the right hand accompanies. Not a device to save for a fugue: it happens constantly in the sonatas, usually at the start of a development. If the piece has a theme and the bass never states it, that is a missed opportunity in every movement.

name: Sforzando punctuation on a weak beat
description: `rest_q [C2,C3]q:sfz rest_h`. A single loud stab where the metre does not expect one. One of the most recognisable Beethoven fingerprints and it costs one note.

name: Octave doubling of the melody
description: both hands on the same line, two or three octaves apart, for a bare unison statement. Use at a theme's most emphatic return, and at the opening of a movement that means to sound severe.

name: Sustained low octave under everything
description: `[C1,C2]w` held for two or four bars while the right hand works above. The bottom of the piano used as a *pedal point*, not as a bass line. Enormous weight for one note.

name: Alberti, deliberately plain
description: `C3e G3e E3e G3e ×2`. Beethoven inherits it and uses it sparingly, usually in an early or a lyrical work. If a whole movement is Alberti it is Mozart's costume, not Beethoven's.

name: Silence
description: `rest_w`. The left hand stops. Beethoven drops the bass out before a return, before a fortissimo, and at the moment a phrase is meant to hang. A whole bar of nothing underneath is a device, not a gap.

name: Contrary-motion scales
description: both hands moving apart or together in scales (`C3e D3e E3e F3e G3e A3e B3e C4e` against a descending right hand). Used at transitions and in codas; it is *motion* rather than accompaniment.

name: Widely-spaced arpeggios
description: the hand covering two octaves per bar: `C2e G2e C3e E3e G3e C4e G3e E3e`. Open, resonant, and characteristic of the later sonatas. Compare with Alberti's narrow oscillation.

name: Off-beat chords with a silent downbeat
description: `rest_e [Eb3,G3]e [Eb3,G3]e [Eb3,G3]e …`. The bar has no floor under its first beat. Unsettling in exactly the way Beethoven likes.

name: The tiny cell
description: a motif of three or four notes, often only a rhythm. Everything grows from it. Write the cell first, then build the theme out of repetitions of it.

name: Motivic fragmentation
description: the theme is stated, then only its first half, then only its first bar, then only its rhythm. Progressive shortening builds tension better than anything else in the vocabulary.

name: Sforzando on a weak beat
description: `C5q:sfz` on beat 2 or 4, or off the beat entirely. Displaces the metre without changing it. One of the most reliable Beethoven fingerprints.

name: Syncopation across the barline
description: a note tied from the last beat of one bar into the next, so the downbeat is not attacked. Sustained over several bars it makes the metre genuinely ambiguous.

name: Sudden dynamic contradiction
description: `ff` followed immediately by `p` with no transition, or a long crescendo that arrives at `pp`. The second is the more characteristic and the more startling.

name: Repeated-note insistence
description: the same pitch struck three, four, six times. Not decoration; it is the argument refusing to move on.

name: The long crescendo over a pedal
description: eight to sixteen bars of intensification over an unchanging bass, arriving at a structural downbeat.

name: Registral extremes juxtaposed
description: a phrase in the deep bass answered immediately two octaves up, with nothing in between.

name: Silence as a downbeat
description: a general pause where the ear expects the strongest beat of the phrase. A whole bar of nothing, then the answer.

name: Trill as an event, not an ornament
description: a long trill sustained over several bars, usually before a return. In the late works it becomes a texture.

name: Accelerating rhythmic values
description: quarters, then eighths, then triplets, then sixteenths across a passage. Acceleration without a tempo change.

name: The wrong-note accent
description: a strong beat carrying a chromatic note that is not in the harmony, marked `sfz`, resolving afterwards.

name: Deceptive cadence, then a second attempt
description: V goes to vi, the phrase starts its cadence again, and only the third attempt lands. Extends a close from two bars to eight.

name: The flattened sixth as a shock
description: ♭VI arriving in place of an expected chord, usually loud and usually at a structural point.

name: Third-related keys
description: moving to the mediant or submediant rather than the dominant. A whole second subject in the mediant is characteristic of the middle and late works.

name: Diminished seventh as a pivot
description: the ambiguous chord used to leave a key abruptly and arrive somewhere remote.

name: Prolonged dominant preparation
description: sixteen or more bars on the dominant before a recapitulation, so the return feels earned rather than scheduled.

name: Neapolitan approach at a moment of pathos
description: ♭II6 before the dominant, in a minor-key slow movement.

name: The false return
description: the theme comes back in the wrong key or too early, and is corrected.

name: Coda as a second development
description: the coda is not a wind-down but the movement's real climax, longer than the exposition's closing group.

name: Thematic transformation across movements
description: the same cell appears in a later movement in a different character. In a multi-movement work this is what makes it one work.

name: Written-out accelerando by note value
description: into a final cadence.
